title: A Kettle in Two Places
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 41 · Lanternweald continuation
content:
By the time I reached Jasmine Steps, Iroh had already decided the missing tea was not missing.

This was a suspicious conclusion to reach while standing beside an empty shelf.

“Observe,” he said, as if he were introducing an elaborate Pai Sho strategy instead of a supply problem.

I observed.

The shelf held nine tins of jasmine tea. The delivery ledger said eleven. The invoice from Ba Sing Se said ten. Somebody had written twelve on the communal kitchen notice board and underlined it twice.

“I observe that nobody in the Lanternweald can count,” I said.

“An unfair accusation. Most people can count beautifully until confronted with tea.”

“You've been making that joke all morning.”

“It improves with repetition.”

“It does not.”

“That is where we disagree.”

He lifted a kettle from the small stove and poured hot water over a pinch of leaves. His stall smelled of jasmine and wood smoke. A ribbon of rain clung to the awning despite the clear blue sky, and one of the lantern brackets above us had developed a greenish line of corrosion.

I wiped a drop from the edge of the shelf.

“This isn't normal weather.”

“No,” he said. “Neri called it Threadrain.”

“Which sounds poetic.”

“Which is often a problem when what one needs is a carpenter.”

I leaned on the counter and looked at the ledger again. The first delivery had been signed before dawn. The second had the same time written in a different hand. Both entries used the same seal.

“Could be a duplicate,” I said.

“Could be theft.”

I looked up.

Iroh's face remained gentle, but there was something older beneath the expression. I had seen that look before, near the city wall. A general assessing a weakness. The habit had not vanished simply because he now served tea.

“Are you worried somebody stole from the stall?”

“I am worried somebody will accuse a hungry neighbor because a ledger is wrong.”

That stopped me.

A boy from Riverstone Terrace had been helping carry deliveries that morning. He was fifteen, too proud to ask for an extra breakfast, and deeply offended by anyone who called him a child. I had offered him bread. He had accepted only after I pretended I had bought too much.

“Some people have already mentioned him,” Iroh said.

“Because he carried the boxes?”

“Because he was seen near an empty shelf. The two facts are not the same.”

I closed the ledger.

“Then we start with the physical crates.”

“Excellent.”

“And nobody gets interrogated over breakfast.”

“A sensible policy for almost every day of the year.”

We went down the terrace to the storeroom beneath the square. The air smelled of damp clay and rosemary. Six delivery crates sat beneath a tarp, their chalk labels streaked where water had reached them. I crouched and lifted the corner of the first.

Someone had marked the same crate twice.

I held up the two tags.

“Here is our thief.”

Iroh considered the tags solemnly.

“A dangerous criminal. We must confiscate its chalk.”

The duplicate labels accounted for one tin. A cracked seal on another crate accounted for the missing second tin: its contents had been transferred to the kitchen when the box began leaking. Nobody had corrected the ledger because everyone believed somebody else had done it.

“An excellent system,” I said.

“Very democratic.”

“That isn't a compliment.”

“I know.”

We were carrying the tins back when Greg appeared from Starwake Pier with a guitar case in one hand and a coil of extension cable in the other. He stopped halfway up the steps.

“Please tell me this is the right place for the community meeting.”

“You've found the tea,” I said. “The meeting is harder to locate.”

“I was told there'd be cake.”

“There may be.”

“Then I'll take my chances.”

Iroh relieved him of the extension cable before he could trip on the stairs.

“Ah, the musician,” he said. “You made the lanterns sing last festival.”

Greg rubbed the back of his neck. “Mostly they rattled in time.”

“An underappreciated instrument.”

They took to each other with alarming speed. Within three minutes they had settled into a debate about whether music could change the taste of tea. Greg said he played better when he had something warm to drink. Iroh said tea tasted better when nobody hurried him. Both seemed to consider this the foundation of an important artistic theory.

I watched them from behind the counter and felt the small, unexpected pleasure of seeing two people I cared about meet as themselves.

Not because either belonged to me.

Because they had found something to talk about without my arranging every word.

Greg offered to help with the benefit concert Neri had proposed. Iroh offered to provide drinks. I offered to prevent both men from volunteering the entire square without discussing the cost.

“An unfriendly position,” Greg said.

“A vital one,” Iroh countered.

The meeting itself was less charming.

Neri put three ruined labels on the table. A Riverstone mason reported that a support had shifted after the rain. Someone from Moonroot said the archive's paper was curling. A Brasswatch volunteer wanted permission to install a locking gate on every Threadway until the weather passed.

“Who would hold the keys?” I asked.

The volunteer hesitated.

“The crew.”

“Which crew?”

“The maintenance crew.”

“And what happens when they're gone, or when somebody needs to leave?”

A murmur moved around the room. It would have been easy for Iroh to resolve the noise with his old commanding voice. I saw him take a breath as though he might.

Then he looked at me.

I let the question stand.

A woman from the kitchen suggested a smaller measure: post safety notices at each door, ask people to close it during storms, repair the lamps, and leave access with the people whose journeys were being affected.

“It won't catch every problem,” she said.

“No rule does,” I answered.

By the end of the meeting we had three volunteers to inspect labels, two to mend the terrace gutters, and a proposal for a better tally system. We also had an argument nobody had settled about private travel records. Neri wrote it on the board with a question mark instead of declaring victory.

That, I thought, was progress.

Back at the stall, Iroh made a fresh pot. His hands moved with the same economy I'd seen when he reset a Pai Sho board after a difficult game.

“You almost gave a speech,” I said.

“I did.”

“Why didn't you?”

“Because I was not certain the room required a general.”

“And what did it require?”

He looked toward the storeroom, where the boy from Riverstone was now eating a bun without an audience.

“A neighbor who could count.”

I smiled.

Iroh set his cup down and took my hand across the counter. His thumb moved once against my palm, warm and familiar.

“Would you come to the Jasmine Dragon tomorrow morning?” he asked.

“I have a meeting at Moonroot after lunch.”

“I asked about morning.”

“You've become very good at asking for the time you actually want.”

“I learned from a difficult person.”

“Tragic.”

“Quite.”

He leaned across the counter. The scent of jasmine rose between us, and for a moment I forgot the damp labels and the meeting and the fact that every door in the vale needed attention. He waited until I leaned closer before kissing me.

It was gentle at first. Then the smile he kept trying to hide made me laugh against his mouth, and he drew back with an expression of exaggerated injury.

“My technique has become amusing?”

“Your timing was excellent. Your beard tickles.”

“An indignity I shall bear.”

We stayed shoulder to shoulder while the last cups dried. At dusk, I walked him to the Jasmine Door. He stepped through toward Ba Sing Se with a promise to send fresh inventory numbers, not a promise that either of us would be in the same place every hour.

Halfway across Lanternwell Square, I noticed the maintenance board.

The two duplicated delivery entries had been written in different inks, but both bore the same smudged time. The paper beneath them was wet only in one narrow vertical stripe, directly below a lantern nobody had inspected yet.

I pressed a finger to the mark.

Cold water touched my skin.

Above me, the lantern glowed in clear air and began to drip.
